questions.question: What is the difference between a reflex action and walking?
answer_steps: A reflex action is sudden, automatic and done without thinking; it is controlled by the spinal cord.
Walking is a voluntary action: we decide to do it, and it is controlled by the brain (with the cerebellum keeping balance).

questions.question: What happens at the synapse between two neurons?
answer_steps: The electrical impulse at the end of the axon releases some chemicals.
These chemicals cross the synapse and start a similar electrical impulse in a dendrite of the next neuron.

questions.question: Which part of the brain maintains posture and equilibrium of the body?
answer_steps: The cerebellum.
It is a part of the hind-brain and also controls the precision of voluntary actions.

questions.question: How do we detect the smell of an agarbatti (incense stick)?
answer_steps: Smell receptors (olfactory receptors) in the nose detect the chemicals of the smoke.
They send impulses through nerves to the fore-brain, which interprets them as the smell of the agarbatti.

questions.question: What is the role of the brain in reflex action?
answer_steps: The reflex action itself is decided in the spinal cord; the brain is not needed for the quick response.
But the information also reaches the brain, which becomes aware of what happened and can use it for thinking and later actions.

questions.question: What are plant hormones?
answer_steps: Plant hormones are chemical compounds made by plants that help to coordinate growth, development and responses to the environment.
Examples: auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid.

questions.question: How is the movement of leaves of the sensitive plant different from the movement of a shoot towards light?
answer_steps: Sensitive plant: the movement is immediate and is not due to growth; cells change shape by changing the amount of water in them.
Shoot towards light: the movement is slow and is due to growth (phototropism).
It is directional, caused by auxin making the cells on the shady side grow longer.

questions.question: Give an example of a plant hormone that promotes growth.
answer_steps: Auxin (it makes cells grow longer).
Gibberellins also promote the growth of the stem.

questions.question: How do auxins promote the growth of a tendril around a support?
answer_steps: When a tendril touches a support, auxin moves to the side away from the support.
The cells on that side grow longer than those touching the support, so the tendril coils around it.

questions.question: Design an experiment to demonstrate hydrotropism.
answer_steps: Plant a few seeds in a box of dry soil, and place a small porous clay pot full of water in the soil on one side.
Water only the clay pot, so water seeps into the soil near it; keep the box in the same conditions for a week.
Dig out the seedlings carefully: the roots will have grown towards the clay pot, showing that roots grow towards water (hydrotropism).

questions.question: How does chemical coordination take place in animals?
answer_steps: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the blood.
The blood carries them to all parts of the body, where they act on specific target cells; their amount is controlled by feedback.

questions.question: Why is the use of iodised salt advisable?
answer_steps: Iodine is needed by the thyroid gland to make the hormone thyroxin, which regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Lack of iodine can cause goitre (a swollen neck).

questions.question: How does our body respond when adrenaline is secreted into the blood?
answer_steps: The heart beats faster, supplying more oxygen to the muscles.
Blood supply to the digestive system and skin is reduced, and blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles.
Breathing becomes faster because of contractions of the diaphragm and rib muscles. All this prepares the body for an emergency.

questions.question: Why are some patients of diabetes treated by giving injections of insulin?
answer_steps: In these patients the pancreas does not secrete enough insulin, so the blood sugar level stays high.
Insulin injections lower the blood sugar level by helping the body use and store glucose.

questions.question: Which of the following is a plant hormone?
questions.explanation: Cytokinins promote cell division in plants; the others are animal hormones.

questions.question: What is the function of receptors in our body? Think of situations where receptors do not work properly. What problems are likely to arise?
answer_steps: Receptors detect information from the environment (light, sound, smell, taste, touch, heat) and pass it to the nervous system as impulses.
If receptors do not work properly, for example the skin's heat receptors are damaged or the nose is blocked by a cold, the information is not detected.
Then the body cannot respond: we may not pull back from a hot object and get burnt, or may not smell gas leaking or food going bad.

questions.question: Draw the structure of a neuron and explain its function.
answer_steps: Labels: dendrites, cell body (with nucleus), axon, and nerve ending.
Dendrites receive information and start an electrical impulse, which travels to the cell body and along the axon.
At the nerve ending, chemicals are released that pass the message across the synapse to the next neuron or to a muscle or gland.

questions.question: How does phototropism occur in plants?
answer_steps: When light falls on a shoot from one side, auxin made at the tip diffuses to the shady side.
Auxin makes the cells on the shady side grow longer, so the shoot bends towards the light.

questions.question: Which signals will get disrupted in case of a spinal cord injury?
answer_steps: Reflex actions controlled by the spinal cord will be disrupted.
Messages between the brain and the body below the injury will also be blocked, so sensations from there will not reach the brain and the brain cannot move those muscles.

questions.question: How does chemical coordination occur in plants?
answer_steps: Plants make hormones (auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid) in one part, which diffuse to the area of action.
These hormones control growth, cell division, bending towards stimuli and wilting, so the plant responds as a whole.

questions.question: What is the need for a system of control and coordination in an organism?
answer_steps: An organism has many organs that must work together, in the right order, to respond to changes in the environment.
Control and coordination make sure the right organs act at the right time, for example the muscles moving the hand away from a flame.

questions.question: How are involuntary actions and reflex actions different from each other?
answer_steps: Involuntary actions, such as the heart beat, breathing and salivation, go on all the time without our thinking; they are controlled by the mid-brain and hind-brain.
Reflex actions are sudden responses to a stimulus, such as pulling back from a hot object; they are controlled by the spinal cord.

questions.question: Compare and contrast nervous and hormonal mechanisms for control and coordination in animals.
answer_steps: Similarity: both pass information from one part of the body to another and coordinate the body's responses.
Nervous: electrical impulses along nerves; very fast; reach only cells connected by nerves; short-lived.
Hormonal: chemicals carried by the blood; slower; reach all cells; steady and long-lasting.

questions.question: What is the difference between the manner in which movement takes place in a sensitive plant and the movement in our legs?
answer_steps: Sensitive plant: there are no nerves or muscles; cells change shape by changing their water content, and the information passes from cell to cell.
Our legs: nerve impulses reach the muscles, whose proteins change shape and arrangement so the muscle fibres shorten, and the legs move.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct combination of function and part of the brain?
questions.explanation: The medulla, in the hind-brain, controls blood pressure; balance is the cerebellum, salivation is the medulla (hind-brain), and hunger is the fore-brain.
option_feedback: Balance is controlled by the cerebellum.
The medulla is in the hind-brain.
The hunger centre is in the fore-brain.

questions.question: The blood glucose level in a patient was very high. It may be due to inadequate secretion of:
questions.explanation: Insulin, made by the pancreas, lowers blood glucose; too little of it causes a high level.
option_feedback: Growth hormone controls growth, not blood sugar.
Insulin is not made by the pituitary.

questions.question: Draw and explain how the nerve cells help in transmission of impulses?
answer_steps: Information is detected at the end of the dendritic tip of a nerve cell, where it sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse.
The impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body, and then along the axon to its end, where it releases some chemicals.

These chemicals cross the synapse and start a similar electrical impulse in a dendrite of the next neuron. (Diagram: two neurons with dendrite, cell body, axon, nerve ending and the synapse between them.)

questions.question: Iodine is necessary for the synthesis of which hormone in the human body?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland uses iodine to make thyroxin.
option_feedback: Growth hormone does not need iodine.

questions.question: Match the plant hormone with its function: Cytokinin
options: Help in the growth of stem
questions.explanation: Cytokinins promote cell division; gibberellins help stem growth; abscisic acid causes wilting.

questions.question: Match the plant hormone with its function: Gibberellins
options: Help in the growth of stem
questions.explanation: Gibberellins help in the growth of the stem.

questions.question: What is Reflex arc? Draw a neat labelled diagram of Reflex arc.
answer_steps: The pathway followed by a reflex action, from the receptor to the effector through the spinal cord, is the reflex arc.
Path: receptor (e.g. in the skin) → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle).
Diagram labels: receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord (with relay neuron), motor neuron, effector muscle.

questions.question: Write a short note on neuron.
answer_steps: A neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.
Parts: dendrites (receive information), cell body (with nucleus), axon (carries the impulse away from the cell body) and nerve ending.
Information starts an electrical impulse at the dendrite; at the nerve ending, chemicals carry it across the synapse to the next cell.

questions.question: In a neuron, the impulse travels in the order:
questions.explanation: Information enters at the dendrite, passes through the cell body and leaves along the axon.
option_feedback: The axon is the exit, not the entry.

questions.question: Reflex arcs are formed in the:
questions.explanation: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord, so reflexes are quick.
option_feedback: The cerebrum is for thinking; reflexes skip it.
The heart is not part of the nervous system.

questions.question: Salivation, vomiting and blood pressure are controlled by the:
questions.explanation: The medulla in the hind-brain controls these involuntary actions.

questions.question: The centre for hunger is located in the:
questions.explanation: The fore-brain has the hunger centre.
option_feedback: The medulla controls blood pressure and salivation.

questions.question: Roots growing downwards is an example of:
questions.explanation: Roots grow towards gravity: positive geotropism.
option_feedback: Roots do grow away from light, but downward growth is a response to gravity.

questions.question: The growth of a pollen tube towards the ovule is:
questions.explanation: The pollen tube grows towards chemicals from the ovule.
option_feedback: That is growth in response to gravity.

questions.question: Which hormone is made at the shoot tip and helps the shoot bend towards light?
questions.explanation: Auxin moves to the shady side and makes those cells grow longer.

questions.question: Which gland secretes growth hormone?
questions.explanation: The pituitary secretes growth hormone.

questions.question: Hormones reach their target cells through:
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, which carries them everywhere.
option_feedback: Nerves carry electrical impulses, not hormones.
The synapse is a gap between neurons.
Hormones are carried by the blood.

questions.question: Deficiency of growth hormone in childhood causes:
questions.explanation: Too little growth hormone causes dwarfism; too much causes gigantism.
option_feedback: Goitre is due to lack of iodine.
Diabetes is due to lack of insulin.
Gigantism is due to too much growth hormone.

questions.question: Name the two parts of the central nervous system and the bony structures that protect them.
answer_steps: The brain, protected by the skull (and a fluid-filled balloon that absorbs shocks).
The spinal cord, protected by the vertebral column (backbone).

questions.question: What is a feedback mechanism? Give an example.
answer_steps: A feedback mechanism regulates the amount and timing of a hormone according to the body's needs.
Example: when blood sugar rises, the pancreas secretes more insulin; as it falls, insulin secretion is reduced.

questions.question: Name the three main parts of the brain and give one function of each.
answer_steps: Fore-brain: thinking, and receiving sensory impulses (also the hunger centre).
Mid-brain: controls some involuntary actions.
Hind-brain: the medulla controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting; the cerebellum controls posture and balance.

questions.question: Name the four plant hormones and give one function of each.
answer_steps: Auxin: makes cells grow longer (shoot bending towards light). Gibberellins: help the stem grow.
Cytokinins: promote cell division.
Abscisic acid: inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves.

questions.question: What is a reflex action? Explain the reflex arc with an example. Why have reflex arcs evolved?
answer_steps: A reflex action is a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus, without thinking.
Example: pulling the hand back on touching a hot object.
Path: heat receptors in the skin → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → muscles of the arm, which pull the hand away.
The information also reaches the brain, so we become aware of it.
Reflex arcs give a very quick response that protects the body from harm, because the slower thinking in the brain is skipped.

questions.question: Name the endocrine glands of the human body and the hormones they secrete. State the effect of deficiency of any two hormones.
answer_steps: Pituitary: growth hormone. Thyroid: thyroxin.
Pancreas: insulin. Adrenal: adrenaline.
Testes: testosterone. Ovaries: oestrogen. Hypothalamus: releasing hormones.
Deficiency of thyroxin (due to lack of iodine): goitre.
Deficiency of insulin: diabetes; deficiency of growth hormone in childhood: dwarfism.

questions.question:
While cooking, Sana accidentally touched a hot pan and pulled her hand away at once. A moment later she felt the pain and said, "That was hot!"

(i) What type of action was pulling the hand away? (1)

(ii) Where was the decision to pull the hand away made? (1)

(iii) Write the path of this action from receptor to effector. OR Why did she feel the pain only after pulling her hand away? (2)
answer_steps: (i) A reflex action.
(ii) In the spinal cord.

(iii) Receptor in the skin → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → arm muscle (effector). OR The quick response was made in the spinal cord; the message took longer to reach the brain, where pain is felt.

questions.question:
A health worker in a hilly village found many people with swollen necks. She advised them to use iodised salt. In the same village, an elderly man was found to have a very high blood sugar level.

(i) Name the disease that causes a swollen neck. (1)

(ii) Which gland is affected in this disease? (1)

(iii) Which hormone is lacking in the elderly man, and which gland makes it? OR How is the secretion of this hormone regulated? (2)
answer_steps: (i) Goitre.
(ii) The thyroid gland.
(iii) Insulin, made by the pancreas. OR By feedback: when blood sugar rises, the pancreas secretes more insulin; as it falls, secretion is reduced.
